title: Progressive Client Contracts & Tool Sandboxing PRD (draft)
content:
Objective:
Provide a lightweight, progressive client contract for the Hosted API that enables secure tool calling and structured streaming for constrained or partially-trusted clients (mobile, embedded, and third-party integrators). The goal is an ergonomic SDK surface + runtime rules that let apps get useful partial results quickly while guaranteeing tool sandboxing, structured output validation, and predictable fallbacks under network or resource degradation.

Context and motivation:
We have many PRDs that focus on streaming semantics and typed tool-handshake for first-class clients. This doc targets a complementary problem: clients with limited memory, intermittent connectivity, or untrusted execution environments that require stronger runtime guards (sandboxing) and simpler SDKs. Examples: mobile chat apps, browser extensions, partner plugins, in-vehicle assistants.

Why this is different:
- Emphasis on client constraints (memory, CPU, battery, unreliable networks) rather than server throughput.
- Built-in tool sandboxing semantics: explicit resource/time budgets, capability scoping, and audited evidence of tool outputs.
- Structured output with progressive validation and compact checkpoints to support offline resume and replay.
- SDK ergonomics optimized for small-footprint language runtimes and JS/Swift/Kotlin idioms.

Success metrics (initial):
- Integration time: first-party app can implement a minimal streaming+tool flow in < 2 dev-days with the SDK.
- Partial-result usefulness: 80% of user flows can surface meaningful partial structured results before full completion in typical mobile networks (p50 ~200ms chunks).
- Safety: zero critical tool-call security incidents in partner integrations in first 6 months.
- Stability: SDK handles client disconnects and resumes session 95% of the time without server-side state leaks.

User personas:
- Mobile product engineer (React Native/Swift): wants simple callbacks, minimal native threading, predictable battery profile.
- Platform partner engineer: needs to sandbox tool invocations (no arbitrary outgoing network calls), audit logs, and offline replay support.
- SDK integrator for a third-party plugin: wants defensive defaults and easy migration path to richer feature set later.

Non‑goals:
- Full-feature parity with our heavyweight streaming SDK (no session mosaic, no microframes initially).
- Support for complex client-side tool graphs. The server will remain the arbiter of orchestration; client gets a declarative subset.

High-level design:
1) Protocol primitives (compact):
   - ProgressiveFrames: minimal framing for partial structured outputs. Each frame contains: sequence_id, schema_version, compact_payload (JSONL or newline-delimited typed tokens), checkpoint_token (opaque), and a signature if tool executed.
   - Lightweight Handshake: client sends a capabilities vector (max_memory_mb, prefer_stream, offline_resume=true/false, allowed_tools list). Server responds with an execution plan: model_id, max_tokens_estimate, allowed_tool_modes (sandboxed|delegated), heartbeat_interval_ms.
   - Sandboxed Tool Calls: when model requests a tool, server emits a ToolCallFrame with tool_id, input_digest (hash), budget_ms, max_outputs, and sandbox_policy_id. The client SDK surfaces a sandbox token to the platform or a signed attestation for third-party executors.

2) Tool sandboxing model:
   - Two principal modes:
     a) Server-Sandboxed: server executes tool and returns signed result. Recommended for untrusted clients. Client only receives signed, verified outputs and checks signature before rendering.
     b) Client-Delegated (sandboxed): client can run local tool under a sandbox runtime (WASM / mobile sandbox) using a short-lived capability token. Token encodes allowed endpoints and quotas. Client must provide attestation of execution (checksum + timestamp) in subsequent frames.
   - Policies: deny-list outgoing domains, restrict local filesystem access, CPU/memory quotas, no persistent background network by default.

3) Structured progressive output and validation:
   - Schema-first approach: server picks a compact schema (short type names) and emits frames with partial validation statuses: tentative | validated | retracted.
   - Checkpoint tokens allow client to re-request missing frames; server will sweep caches for replay within a bounded TTL (default 5 minutes for hosted flow, configurable for Dedicated).
   - Compact deltas: to reduce mobile bandwidth, frames can contain delta updates to previous JSON paths rather than full objects. SDK exposes a small path-merge utility.

4) SDK ergonomics (surface & patterns):
   - Two-level API: SimpleFlow and AdvancedFlow.
     * SimpleFlow (recommended for constrained clients): one callback onPartial(structuredFragment) and one onComplete(fullStructuredDoc). No tool exposure unless server-sandboxed.
     * AdvancedFlow: exposes toolCall requests with a safe runTool(toolManifest, input, opts) promise that will enforce sandbox policies.
   - Backpressure and batching: SDK buffers incoming partial frames and exposes adaptive flush controls. Default low-memory mode batches up to N frames or M ms (configurable).
   - Resume & replay: SDK persists checkpoint_token + minimal serialized last_validated_fragment to secure local storage. On reconnection, SDK issues a resume request with token and plays missing frames into the same callbacks.

API sketches (pseudocode):
- SimpleFlow (JS):
  const flow = HostedSDK.startSimpleFlow({model: 'redwood-compact-llm', offlineResume: true});
  flow.onPartial(fragment => renderDelta(fragment));
  flow.onComplete(doc => commit(doc));
  flow.onError(err => fallbackToNonStreaming(err));

- AdvancedFlow (JS) tool call hook:
  flow.onToolRequest(async req => {
    // server asked to run 'lookup' tool with sandbox policy 7
    if (req.sandboxMode === 'server-sandboxed') return await flow.fetchSignedToolResult(req.callId);
    // delegate locally in a restricted runtime
    const attestation = await localWasmRunner.run(req.toolId, req.input, {cpuMs: req.budgetMs});
    return {attestation, output: attestation.output};
  });

Observability and telemetry:
- Minimal telemetry emitted by SDK: handshake_summary, resume_attempts, tool_attestations_count, partial_frames_received, average_fragment_size.
- All tool-call events must be recorded server-side; signed-tool results include server signature chain for audit.

Security & privacy considerations:
- Default to server-sandboxed tool execution for any untrusted or third-party client.
- Tokens are short-lived (<= 2 minutes) and audience-restricted.
- SDK must not persist tool inputs/outputs unless developer opts-in; opt-in requires explicit policy audit.

Rollout plan (phases):
- Phase 0 (internal): small dev preview with Redwood mobile team, server-sandboxed only. Collect latency, partiality, and resume metrics. (4 weeks)
- Phase 1 (partners): enable client-delegated sandbox tokens for vetted partners with auditing tools. Add WASM runner sample. (8 weeks)
- Phase 2 (public): GA with both flows, SDKs on npm/CocoaPods/Maven and default to SimpleFlow for new integrations. (6 weeks)

Open questions / risks:
- How large should default checkpoint TTL be for hosted API vs Dedicated? (Cost vs reliability tradeoff)
- Audit surface: do we need deterministic attestation formats (e.g., CWT/JWT with embedded hashes) or is an opaque signed blob acceptable?
- UX: how to surface tool-sandbox failures to end-users without exposing internal error codes?
- SDK size constraints on low-end Android devices; can we keep JS SDK + small native shim < 200KB gzipped?

Action items (owners):
- Prototype compact frame encoding (Evelyn) — due 2025-10-01.
- Server-sandbox signed tool result format proposal (Diego) — JIRA-API-867 — due 2025-09-26.
- Minimal mobile SDK SimpleFlow implement (Maya) — PR to hosted-sdk repo and sample RN app — due 2025-10-15.

References and links:
- see linked artifacts above (CONFLUENCE-CC-42 for design notes, JIRA-API-867 for server tool signing).
- Slack thread: #prod-hosted-api streaming-handshake (recent discussion 2025-09-10).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally conservative on orchestration and favors server authority for safety. Feedback sought on the balance between server-sandbox vs client-delegated performance tradeoffs and on SDK footprint targets.
